gobekli-tepe.title: Architecture at human scale.
gobekli-tepe.intro: Two close views move from the overall monument to the architectural details that make Göbekli Tepe legible as a built environment rather than an abstract archaeological icon.

images.label: Building B
images.title: Göbeklitepe Building B
images.caption: A round-plan building roughly 10 metres in diameter, with T-shaped limestone pillars arranged around the wall and two central monoliths. Fox reliefs appear on the inward-facing sides of the central pillars.
images.alt: Round-plan Building B at Göbekli Tepe with T-shaped limestone pillars
images.creator: Dosseman

images.label: Building D
images.title: Göbeklitepe Building D
images.caption: The best-preserved monumental enclosure at the site. Its two central pillars survive to about 5.5 metres and carry anthropomorphic details including arms, hands, belts and loincloths.
images.alt: Building D at Göbekli Tepe with monumental central T-shaped pillars
images.creator: Dosseman

hattusa.title: Power in stone and landscape.
hattusa.intro: Hattusa is easier to understand when the royal citadel and the nearby rock sanctuary are seen together: political space inside the city and ritual space extending beyond it.

images.label: Royal citadel
images.title: Büyükkale, Buildings C and H
images.caption: Remains on Büyükkale, the royal citadel, where renewed excavation and radiocarbon work are refining the chronology of palace expansion and the Upper City.
images.alt: Stone remains of Buildings C and H on the Büyükkale citadel at Hattusa
images.creator: Carole Raddato

images.label: Yazılıkaya
images.title: Twelve Underworld Gods, Chamber B
images.caption: A procession of twelve male underworld deities carved into the rock of Chamber B at Yazılıkaya, the sanctuary that extends Hattusa's ritual landscape beyond the fortified city.
images.alt: Rock-cut procession of twelve underworld deities in Chamber B at Yazılıkaya
images.creator: Ywpark2003

catalhoyuk.title: The house as an archive.
catalhoyuk.intro: The strongest visual evidence at Çatalhöyük is interior: painted surfaces, platforms, installations and reconstructed spatial relationships show how architecture accumulated memory through repeated use.

images.label: Painted surface
images.title: Çatalhöyük wall painting
images.caption: A surviving wall painting now in the Konya Archaeological Museum. Painted and replastered surfaces were repeatedly renewed as part of the life histories of houses.
images.alt: Neolithic wall painting from Çatalhöyük displayed in the Konya Archaeological Museum
images.creator: Dosseman

images.label: Reconstruction
images.title: Reconstructed Çatalhöyük room
images.caption: A museum reconstruction using original finds in relative position to communicate the close relationship between roof-entry architecture, interior platforms and below-floor burial practices.
images.alt: Reconstructed Neolithic room from Çatalhöyük in the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations
images.creator: Dosseman
